messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: student-t and Matt trick
parts:
I tried estimating some models using a student t instead of a normal.
The was to match my expectation that most effects would be ~0, but a few
might be notable.

It didn't work too well. I wonder if part of the problem is that the
specification of a variable df undercuts the Matt trick, since even the
_raw parameters are now changing scale.

Is there anything to that? Is there a way around it, for example
altering the sd of the _raw distribution to offset the scale changes
induced by the df? Unfortunately that isn't possible for df<2 (since t
has no finite variance there). Maybe restrict df to be >2?

Some details:

First try: fix df for t at 1. A total disaster: after 7 hours I had a
minimum n_eff of 2!

Second try: allow df to have a cauchy(0, 5) prior. This took only 0.3
hours, but n_eff was only 24 (and this from 3000 iterations
post-warmup).

The estimation code for the second try included this (excerpts only)
parameters {
matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
vector<lower=0>[NSD] df; // df for t distn
}
transformed parameters {
matrix [J, K] beta;
for(ir in 1:J)
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
}
model {
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
df ~ cauchy(0, 5);
for(ir in 1:J)
beta_raw[ir] ~ student_t(df[SDClass[ir]], 0, 1);
}

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] student-t and Matt trick [hierarchical dof + scale]
parts:
Some comments below, but you really need Matt or Michael
helping with this one. Or maybe Andrew's had some experience
with hierarchical Student-t priors.

On 10/10/13 2:19 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> I tried estimating some models using a student t instead of a normal.
> The was to match my expectation that most effects would be ~0, but a few
> might be notable.
>
> It didn't work too well. I wonder if part of the problem is that the
> specification of a variable df undercuts the Matt trick, since even the
> _raw parameters are now changing scale.

As Matt likes to say, that was "a Matt trick", not "the Matt trick".
I don't know how well it'll work here, but you can take the Student-t
apart into component normal and chi-square distributions:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student's_t-distribution#As_the_distribution_of_a_test_statistic

Another Matt trick did the same kind of thing for gamma distributions.

> Is there anything to that? Is there a way around it, for example
> altering the sd of the _raw distribution to offset the scale changes
> induced by the df? Unfortunately that isn't possible for df<2 (since t
> has no finite variance there). Maybe restrict df to be >2?
If you make df big enough, you're back to roughly normal :-)

> Some details:
>
> First try: fix df for t at 1. A total disaster: after 7 hours I had a
> minimum n_eff of 2!

I'm not sure why that would be so problematic. Fixing df=1 just
gives you the Cauchy distribution. But even there, the sampler
can wander off into the tails, which have a rather different scale
for the Cauchy than the central part. Did the traceplots wander up into
high values?

> Second try: allow df to have a cauchy(0, 5) prior. This took only 0.3
> hours, but n_eff was only 24 (and this from 3000 iterations
> post-warmup).

If that's as bad as it gets, that's about an hour and fifteen
minutes to get 100 effective samples.

Were the results sensible?

On Thu, Oct 10, 2013 at 08:49:08PM +0200, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Indeed, I doubt it makes sense to have independent priors on sigma_beta and df. You might try parameterizing as sigma_beta <- scale*(df-2)/df, and then having scale and df be independent. Also, I don't think your prior for df is so good.

Out of curiosity, since I take the advice to be changing the
parameterization, what would a better prior have been?

Bob asked if the results were reasonable; I didn't look at them too
closely, but they didn't look too bad. The df distributions had a
large tail, which actually may be part of the problem: the scale for
df is highly elastic, with small changes making a big difference at
the bottom but having almost no effect for large values:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
sigma_beta[1] 1.1 0 0.3 0.5 0.8 1.0 1.3 1.8 61 1.1
sigma_beta[2] 0.4 0 0.1 0.3 0.3 0.4 0.4 0.5 127 1.0
sigma_beta[3] 0.2 0 0.0 0.1 0.2 0.2 0.2 0.3 74 1.0

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
df[1] 36.8 7.2 328.5 1.2 4.6 8.5 19.8 223.7 2085 1
df[2] 48.9 7.9 272.1 3.2 7.4 12.8 29.8 276.4 1180 1
df[3] 28.8 6.9 156.1 2.0 4.7 8.3 16.7 175.3 509 1

df[1] and sigma_beta[1] go together, for example.

Looking just at the medians for df I think the t's end up being pretty close to normal.

It was also interesting that, among the parameters with the very worst
n_eff (<50), most were _raw; relatively few of the transformed
versions were as weak. In particular, there were no transformed beta
parameters in this group (beta=effects of covariates vs alpha effects
of cluster).

Ross

On 10/10/13 3:32 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 10, 2013 at 08:49:08PM +0200, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> Indeed, I doubt it makes sense to have independent priors on sigma_beta and df. You might try parameterizing as sigma_beta <- scale*(df-2)/df, and then having scale and df be independent. Also, I don't think your prior for df is so good.
>
> Out of curiosity, since I take the advice to be changing the
> parameterization, what would a better prior have been?

Andrew leaves these tantalizing hints. Maybe he'll clarify.

...

> It was also interesting that, among the parameters with the very worst
> n_eff (<50), most were _raw; relatively few of the transformed
> versions were as weak. In particular, there were no transformed beta
> parameters in this group (beta=effects of covariates vs alpha effects
> of cluster).

I don't know what to make of this. On the one hand, the non-raw ones
are what we care about. On the other, the _raw ones are what is actually
being sampled by the sampler.

One case where you really don't care about the raw values is when
they aren't properly identified compared to the transformed versions.

> P.S. Who is Matt?

Matt Hoffman:

http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~mdhoffma/

He invented NUTS, which is Stan's default sampler.

He also invented stochastic variational inference, which we're
working on building into Stan.

- Bob

parts:
I'm not sure the best prior for df, but I assume you'd want to restrict df to be greater than 1 or even to restrict to be greater than 2. One possibility could be an exponential distribution on (df-1) or (df-2) with scale 5.
In the past I've tried parameterizing on 1/df but that doesn't seem quite right either.
A

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] student-t and Matt trick
parts:
On Thu, 2013-10-10 at 22:02 +0200, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I'm not sure the best prior for df, but I assume you'd want to restrict df to be greater than 1 or even to restrict to be greater than 2. One possibility could be an exponential distribution on (df-1) or (df-2) with scale 5.
> In the past I've tried parameterizing on 1/df but that doesn't seem quite right either.
> A

I put the above suggestion with that of earlier emails, and the results
are still not very good. I did apply a sqrt to the variance
normalization, which seemed right for a scale parameter. There was a
floor of 2.01 on the df values.

Running 3 parallel chains of 2000 iterations each, reducing the warmup
to 500, ended up with a minimum n_eff of 11 (though Q1 of n_eff was >
2,000). About 2/3 hour wall time. The substantive estimates I checked
looked pretty much the same as with the normal model.

I guess in this case, relative simplicity wins.

The parameter with the lowest n_eff (one of the beta) had an odd trace:
one of the chains showed much higher variability than the others (also
the worst Rhat at 1.11). None of the chains looked stuck. All the
chains looked very similar during warmup; it was only after that they
diverged. The relevant df and scale parameters are very low and very
high respectively during the periods of high variability of the beta in
that chain. However, the other chains also exhibit periods of low
beta/high scale.

Maybe moving the floor of the df even higher would prevent the extreme
scale values they produce. It looks as if the attempt to separate
sigma_beta into independent parameters for scale and df didn't work; df
and scale appear more coupled than df and sigma_beta.

Here's the code, if anyone is curious:
data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of partners
int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race
// K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
int<lower=0> J; //number of covariates
int<lower=0> NSD; // number of classes of beta for sd
int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J]; // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N]; // partner race
int<lower=0> NCLUSTER; //number of respondents
int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
row_vector[J] x[N]; // covariates

}
parameters {
matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients

vector[K] alpha_raw[NCLUSTER]; // cluster effects
real<lower=0> sigma;
real<lower=0> scale_beta[NSD];
vector<lower=0>[NSD] df_raw; // df for t distn minimum value 2.01

}
transformed parameters {
matrix [J, K] beta;

vector[K] alpha[NCLUSTER];
vector<lower=0>[NSD] sigma_beta;
for (i in 1:NSD)
sigma_beta[i] <- scale_beta[i]*sqrt((df_raw[i]+.01)/(df_raw[i]+2.01));

for(ir in 1:J)
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];

for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i]*sigma;
}
model {
vector[K] beta_x;
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
scale_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
df_raw ~ exponential(0.2);
for(ir in 1:J)
beta_raw[ir] ~ student_t(2.01+df_raw[SDClass[ir]], 0, 1);
for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
alpha_raw[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
for(n in 1:N) {
beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)'+alpha[iCluster[n]];
pEthnic[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta_x);
}
}

3 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=500; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=1500, total post-warmup draws=4500.
mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] student-t and Matt trick
parts:
R
One take on this is that t-distribution errors could be thought of as arising from a mixture model, in which case that mixture distribution can be modeled directly.
It is known that low-df t models can have convergence problems because of multimodality, which in some sense can be thought of as discrete aspects of the mixture model.
A

P.S. Thanks for interacting on this. The discussion is helpful to me.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] student-t and Matt trick
parts:
To expand on Andrew's point:

One thing that sometimes works when you're having trouble with the
heavy-tailedness of student-t distributions is to use the
gamma-mixture representation:

beta ~ student_t(nu, 0, 1);
<=>
tau ~ gamma(nu/2, nu/2);
beta ~ normal(0, 1/sqrt(tau)).

That is, the marginal distribution of beta when you integrate out tau
is student_t(nu, 0, 1). You can take this a step further and say that

mu <- x * beta;
beta ~ student_t(nu, 0, 1);
<=>
tau ~ gamma(nu/2, nu/2);
beta_01 ~ normal(0, 1)
mu <- x * beta_01 / sqrt(tau).

Marginally, mu has the same distribution under these models, but in
the first parameterization beta has (potentially) heavy tails, whereas
in the second neither tau nor beta_01 have heavy tails.

So it might help to try it that way. Of course, it might not.

Best,
Matt
